rv.q: The resulting tragedy has a snarling, pent-up energy.
Engaging, deliberately paced take on the classic study of class conflict and cruelty
Marber's reimagining may be the best of them all, its psychosexual dynamics teetering on a 70 minutes long tightrope.

Her Julie exuded a sexy, demanding confidence while allowing flashes of excruciating vulnerability and longing to surface. At times spoilt and petulant, at others poised and refined, this Julie possessed a troubling masochistic streak and emotional volatility, revealing a deeply fractured, childlike psyche.
When the tensions fail to ignite, the emotional core remains hidden, leaving a sense of promise unfulfilled.

The result is a lead directorial debut by Lin which is an incredibly tight piece of work. She stages Patrick Marber’s play in the round, making it all the more scrutinous. This choice is a great accompaniment to the story’s portrayal of the post-war British class system, also allowing for some subtly spectacular visual moments.
In just under seventy minutes, this production delivered a textbook lesson in precision.
Marber's adaptation remains thought-provoking and thematically rich.

cn.t: Marber's adaptation of Strindberg earns mostly positive notices for its precision and psychosexual tension, though some critics find the emotional core doesn't fully ignite in this brisk 70-minute production.
